a: Rules of thumb: roughly 10^8 simple operations per second. n ≤ 20 → exponential/backtracking is fine. n ≤ 5,000 → O(n²) is fine. n around 10^5 to 10^6 → you need O(n log n) or O(n). Sorting is O(n log n); heap push/pop O(log n); hash operations O(1) average; binary search O(log n).
Space counts too: recursion depth is stack space, and many DP tables compress to two rows.
Practice reps live in vizly DSA Quest; this section is recall only.
topics.example: n = 10^5 with a nested loop = 10^10 operations: guaranteed timeout. That number alone tells you to reach for sort + two pointers, a hash map, or a heap to drop a factor of n before writing any code.

a: A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime: a few KB of stack, multiplexed onto OS threads by the scheduler (M:N), so hundreds of thousands are fine. Started with the go keyword.

Channels are typed pipes between goroutines: 'share memory by communicating, not communicate by sharing memory.' Unbuffered channel: send blocks until a receiver is ready (a synchronization point). Buffered channel: send blocks only when the buffer is full. close(ch) signals no more values; range over a channel reads until it is closed.
topics.example: Worker pool: jobs := make(chan Job, 100). Start 10 goroutines that do 'for job := range jobs { process(job) }'. The producer sends jobs and calls close(jobs) when done; a sync.WaitGroup waits for all workers to finish.

a: select waits on multiple channel operations and runs whichever is ready first: the core tool for timeouts, cancellation and multiplexing. context.Context carries deadlines and cancellation down a call chain; every blocking call should respect ctx.Done(). Cancel a parent context and everything below it stops.

sync package: Mutex/RWMutex for shared state, WaitGroup to wait for a set of goroutines, Once for one-time init. errgroup (golang.org/x/sync) combines WaitGroup with error propagation and context cancellation.
topics.example: HTTP handler: ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second); defer cancel(). Pass ctx into the DB query. If the client disconnects or 2s pass, the query is cancelled instead of leaking a goroutine.

a: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly: any type with the matching methods implements the interface, no 'implements' keyword. This keeps packages decoupled: define the interface where it is used (the consumer), not where it is implemented.
Idioms: keep interfaces small (io.Reader has one method), 'accept interfaces, return structs.' There is no inheritance: reuse comes from struct embedding (composition).
topics.example: The orders package defines: type Notifier interface { Notify(ctx context.Context, msg string) error }. EmailNotifier and SlackNotifier satisfy it automatically just by having that method, and never need to import the orders package.

a: Errors are plain values returned as the last result and checked with if err != nil. No exceptions for normal control flow. Wrap errors with context: fmt.Errorf("fetch user %d: %w", id, err); inspect the chain with errors.Is (sentinel match) and errors.As (type match).
panic/recover is only for truly unrecoverable states, never for expected failures like a missing row. defer runs cleanup on the way out (close files, unlock mutexes) in LIFO order.
topics.example: if errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) { return nil, ErrUserNotFound }. The repository translates a driver-level error into a domain error, and the HTTP handler maps that domain error to a 404.

a: A slice is a small header (pointer, length, capacity) over a backing array: two slices can share the same array, so a write through one is visible in the other. append may reallocate, so always assign the result back. Maps are not safe for concurrent writes: guard with a mutex or use sync.Map.

Runtime: concurrent mark-and-sweep GC tuned for sub-millisecond pauses, GOMAXPROCS controls parallelism. Go compiles to one static binary, which is why Go container images are tiny (FROM scratch works).
topics.example: b := a[:2] then b = append(b, x): if a had spare capacity, x silently overwrites a[2]. Classic interview gotcha. Safe copy: c := make([]int, len(a)); copy(c, a).

a: STAR: Situation (one sentence of context), Task (what YOU owned), Action (what YOU did: 70% of the answer, say 'I' not 'we'), Result (quantified outcome + what you learned). Keep the whole answer 2-3 minutes.

Prepare 6-8 stories before interviews and map them to the usual questions: hardest technical problem, conflict with a colleague, failure/mistake, tight deadline, mentoring someone, disagreeing with a decision, leading without authority. One strong story can serve multiple questions from different angles.
Quantify results: '82M requests/month', 'cut p99 from 800ms to 120ms', 'onboarding time from 2 weeks to 3 days'. Numbers make stories credible and memorable.
topics.example: 'Tell me about a production issue you owned': Situation: checkout errors spiked at peak. Task: I was on call and led the incident. Action: I checked the RED dashboard, traced it to pool exhaustion, applied a bulkhead + capped pools, wrote the postmortem. Result: 40 minutes of impact, and the class of incident never recurred; the fix became a platform default.

a: Senior roles are expected to mentor, so have concrete answers ready. Mentoring: pair on real tickets rather than lecture, give the junior a slightly-too-big task with a safety net, do regular 1:1s, measure success by them not needing you anymore.

Code review philosophy: review for correctness, tests and design first, style last (linters own style). Distinguish blocking issues from nitpicks explicitly ('nit:' prefix). Comment on the code, never the person; ask questions instead of commanding ('what happens if this times out?'). Big PRs get a synchronous walkthrough instead of 200 comments.
Senior signal: you raise the team's level (docs, patterns, onboarding), not just your own output.
topics.example: Question: 'A junior keeps submitting buggy PRs, what do you do?' Answer shape: first pair with them privately to find the real gap (testing habits? domain knowledge?), agree on a pre-PR checklist, pair-write tests for the next feature, then track improvement over a month before involving the manager.

a: Disagreement pattern interviewers want: you argued with data and prototypes, not volume; you genuinely listened to the other side; a decision got made (by you, consensus or escalation); then you committed fully even if it wasn't your choice: disagree and commit.

Ambiguity (a standard senior-role requirement): show a bias for reversible action. Timebox research, write a one-page proposal with options and a recommendation, pick the reversible option when unsure, set a checkpoint to revisit. Never 'I waited for someone to decide.'
Escalation is not failure: escalating a stuck decision with a clear write-up of both options is a senior move.
topics.example: 'I pushed for Postgres, a teammate wanted MongoDB. I wrote a one-pager comparing both against our access patterns and ran a load test on the riskiest query. We picked Postgres, but their concern about schema churn was valid, so we added a jsonb column for the volatile attributes. Shipped on time; both of us owned the result.'

topics.q: Go, Ruby/Rails, Java/JVM, Python Quick Notes
a: Go: compiled to one static binary, goroutines make high concurrency cheap (no GIL/GVL equivalent), low memory footprint and fast startup: the default pick for new microservices, proxies and infra tooling. Small language by design: little magic, fast onboarding, but more boilerplate than Rails/Django. The dedicated Go section above covers it in depth.

Ruby/Rails: MRI has a GVL (global VM lock), so one process runs one thread of Ruby at a time; scaling is multi-process (Puma workers) plus threads for I/O. Rails = convention over configuration: ActiveRecord ORM (watch N+1: use includes), migrations, Sidekiq (Redis-backed) for background jobs. Many delivery and e-commerce companies still run a Rails monolith, so expect at least respect-level questions.

Java/JVM: real OS threads (virtual threads since 21 for cheap concurrency), generational GC (G1 default, ZGC for low pause), JIT warms up hot paths. Spring Boot: DI container, @Transactional, heavy but battle-tested for large teams.

Python: GIL means threads don't help CPU-bound work: use multiprocessing or async I/O (FastAPI/asyncio) for concurrency. Type hints + mypy for large codebases. Common in tooling, data and ML services around a Go/Java core.
Interview stance: 'strongest in Go/Node, productive quickly in the others, and the fundamentals (DB, HTTP, testing, design) transfer.' Then prove it with these specifics.
topics.example: Question: 'Rails app is slow under load, what do you check?' Answer: N+1 queries via the log (bullet gem), missing indexes, GVL contention meaning too few Puma workers, slow external calls without timeouts inside request threads, then cache fragments/queries. Same playbook as any stack, named in Rails terms.
